unit: Unit 7: Contract of Indemnity and Guarantee
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Contract of Indemnity and Rights of Indemnity-Holder
explain: Indemnity means to compensate for loss or make good the financial damage caused to another.
Under Section 124, it is a contract where one party promises to save the other from loss caused by the promisor or any other person.
There are two parties: Indemnifier (person giving the promise) and Indemnified/Indemnity-holder (person receiving protection).
Section 124 covers losses caused by human conduct; accidents and acts of God are excluded from this specific statutory definition.
Under Section 125, when sued, an indemnity-holder acting within authority can recover all damages, suit costs, and compromise amounts.
The indemnifier's liability commences as soon as the liability of the indemnity-holder becomes absolute and certain.

flow.title: How Indemnity Claim Works
steps: Indemnity contract executed between parties
Loss occurs due to human conduct
Indemnity-holder liability becomes absolute and certain
Indemnity-holder demands reimbursement from indemnifier
Indemnifier pays damages costs and compromise sums

topics.example: Mr. X promises to reimburse the Government if he fails to return to India after his Govt-funded studies at Cambridge.
remember: Section 124 covers loss by conduct of promisor or third party
Fire and Marine insurance are indemnity contracts, but Life insurance is not
mistakes: Assuming acts of God or natural accidents are covered under Section 124 statutory definition
Believing an illegal object (like promising indemnity to beat someone) can form a valid indemnity contract

quiz.q: Under Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, a contract of indemnity covers loss caused by:
o: Acts of God and natural calamities only
Conduct of the promisor or any other person
Accidents unrelated to human intervention
Every possible future event including death
quiz.why: Section 124 specifically restricts the definition to loss caused by the conduct of the promisor or another person.

quiz.q: When does the liability of an indemnifier commence according to judicial rulings?
o: Only after the indemnified actually pays cash out of pocket
As soon as the liability of the indemnity-holder becomes absolute and certain
When the contract is signed by both parties
Only upon a decree passed by the Supreme Court
quiz.why: Judicial pronouncements state liability begins as soon as the indemnity-holder's liability becomes absolute and certain.

topics.title: Contract of Guarantee and Essential Features
explain: A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of default.
Three parties are involved: Principal Debtor (who defaults), Creditor (to whom guarantee is given), and Surety (who gives guarantee).
It involves three contracts: Principal contract (PD & Creditor), Secondary contract (Creditor & Surety), and Implied contract (Surety & PD).
Under Section 127, consideration given to the principal debtor is sufficient consideration for the surety; past consideration is invalid.
If the principal debtor is a minor, the guarantee remains valid, but if the surety is a minor, the guarantee is void.
Guarantee obtained by misrepresentation (Sec 142) or concealment of material facts (Sec 143) is invalid.

flow.title: Structure of a Guarantee Agreement
steps: Principal Debtor requests loan or goods from Creditor
Creditor asks for a guarantee to secure debt
Surety provides guarantee to Creditor for PD default
Creditor extends credit to Principal Debtor
Implied duty arises for PD to indemnify Surety

topics.example: A requests B to lend ₹10,000 to C, promising that if C fails to pay, A will pay B. A is the surety, B is creditor, C is principal debtor.
remember: Guarantee requires an existing enforceable principal debt
Past consideration is no consideration for a guarantee contract
Guarantee can be oral or written (Section 126)
mistakes: Thinking a guarantee is void if the principal debtor is incompetent to contract
Confusing past consideration with valid consideration for a surety's promise

quiz.q: What is the legal effect if a guarantee is given for a principal debtor who is a minor?
o: The contract of guarantee is completely void
The contract of guarantee remains valid and enforceable against the surety
The creditor must first sue the minor in court
The surety is discharged from all liability
quiz.why: Even if the principal debtor is incompetent to contract, the guarantee given by a competent surety remains valid.

quiz.q: Under Section 127, which of the following acts as valid consideration for a surety's guarantee?
o: Past benefit conferred on the principal debtor long ago
Anything done or promise made for the benefit of the principal debtor
A direct cash payment made directly to the surety by the creditor
Moral obligation of the surety toward the debtor
quiz.why: Section 127 states consideration received by the principal debtor is sufficient consideration for the surety.

topics.title: Types of Guarantees: Specific vs. Continuing
explain: A Specific Guarantee extends to a single debt or one specific transaction; liability ends when that debt is paid.
A Continuing Guarantee under Section 129 extends to a series of transactions over a period of time.
In a continuing guarantee, surety's liability applies to the unpaid balance at the end of the guaranteed scope.
A continuing guarantee can be revoked by notice to the creditor (Section 130) for future transactions.
Death of the surety (Section 131) automatically revokes a continuing guarantee regarding future transactions unless contracted otherwise.

flow.title: Operation and Revocation of Continuing Guarantee
steps: Surety gives guarantee for ongoing series of supplies
Multiple credit transactions occur between Creditor and Debtor
Surety issues notice of revocation or surety dies
Guarantee terminates for all future transactions
Surety remains liable for past transactions before notice

topics.example: A guarantees payment to B (tea dealer) up to ₹10,000 for any tea supplied to C from time to time. This is a continuing guarantee.
remember: Revocation applies ONLY to future transactions
mistakes: Believing revocation of a continuing guarantee cancels liability for transactions already completed before notice
Treating a guarantee for a single loan payable in installments as a continuing guarantee

quiz.q: A guarantee which extends to a series of transactions is called a:
o: Specific guarantee
Absolute indemnity
Continuing guarantee
Retrospective guarantee
quiz.why: Section 129 defines a guarantee that extends to a series of transactions as a continuing guarantee.

quiz.q: Upon the death of a surety, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, a continuing guarantee is:
o: Revoked for both past and future transactions
Revoked only as to future transactions
Not revoked at all and continues for future transactions
Converted into a specific guarantee
quiz.why: Under Section 131, death revokes a continuing guarantee for future transactions, leaving the estate liable for past acts.

topics.title: Distinction Between Contract of Indemnity and Guarantee
explain: Indemnity has 2 parties (Indemnifier & Indemnified); Guarantee has 3 parties (Surety, Principal Debtor, Creditor).
Indemnity has 1 contract; Guarantee has 3 contracts (Principal, Secondary, and Implied).
Indemnifier's liability is primary and unconditional; Surety's liability is secondary and conditional on debtor's default.
Indemnifier liability arises on a contingency; Surety liability arises on non-performance of an existing debt.
Indemnifier cannot sue a third party in own name without assignment; Surety can sue debtor directly after paying debt.

flow.title: Comparing Core Structure
steps: Indemnity: 2 Parties -> 1 Contract -> Primary Liability
Guarantee: 3 Parties -> 3 Contracts -> Secondary Liability
Indemnifier acts independently without debtor request
Surety acts specifically at request of Principal Debtor

topics.example: If A promises to save B from loss in a lawsuit, it is Indemnity. If A promises C to pay B's loan if B defaults, it is Guarantee.
mistakes: Thinking the indemnifier can sue a third party directly without an express assignment of rights
Assuming a surety's liability is primary instead of secondary

quiz.q: How many contracts exist in a valid tripartite Contract of Guarantee?
o: One contract
Two contracts
Three contracts
Four contracts
quiz.why: A guarantee involves three contracts: between debtor & creditor, creditor & surety, and surety & debtor.

quiz.q: What is the nature of the indemnifier's liability in a contract of indemnity?
o: Secondary and conditional
Primary and unconditional
Co-extensive with co-sureties
Voidable at option of promisee
quiz.why: The liability of an indemnifier is primary and unconditional, arising directly upon the happening of the loss.

topics.title: Nature and Extent of Surety's Liability
explain: Under Section 128, the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless provided otherwise.
Co-extensive means the surety is liable for the exact amount the debtor owes, including interest and charges upon default.
Surety's liability is secondary; it gets triggered only when the principal debtor defaults.
The creditor is not required to sue the principal debtor first; the creditor can proceed against the surety directly.
Under Section 132, if two joint debtors agree between themselves that one is surety, creditor's right to enforce primary liability against both is unaffected.

flow.title: Enforcing Surety Liability
steps: Principal Debtor defaults on payment obligation
Surety liability gets triggered (Secondary nature)
Creditor chooses to sue Surety directly without suing Debtor
Surety pays full debt plus interest and default charges
Surety seeks recovery from Principal Debtor

topics.example: A guarantees B's bill of exchange accepted by C. C dishonours it. A is liable for the principal amount plus accrued interest and charges.
remember: Surety liability is co-extensive with principal debtor (Section 128)
Creditor can sue surety without suing principal debtor first
mistakes: Thinking a creditor MUST sue the principal debtor before suing the surety
Assuming surety liability excludes interest or penalty charges when debtor defaults

quiz.q: According to Section 128, the liability of the surety is ________ with that of the principal debtor.
o: Less than
Co-extensive
Independent
Unrelated
quiz.why: Section 128 explicitly states that surety liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor unless agreed otherwise.

quiz.q: If debtor C defaults on a loan guaranteed by A to creditor B, B can:
o: Only sue C and wait for court execution
Sue A directly without first suing C
Not claim any interest from A
Cancel the contract immediately without remedy
quiz.why: A creditor may choose to proceed against the surety directly upon default, unless the contract specifies otherwise.

topics.title: Discharge of a Surety
explain: A surety is discharged when their legal liability comes to an end under three broad modes.
1. By Revocation: Notice for future transactions (Sec 130), Death of surety (Sec 131), or Novation (Sec 62).

2. By Conduct of Creditor: Variance in contract terms without surety consent (Sec 133); Release of debtor (Sec 134); Creditor compounding, giving time, or promising not to sue debtor (Sec 135); Creditor impairing surety's remedy (Sec 139).
3. By Invalidation: Guarantee obtained by misrepresentation (Sec 142), concealment (Sec 143), or failure of co-surety to join (Sec 144).
Not Discharged: Creditor making agreement with a third party to give time to debtor (Sec 136), or creditor's mere forbearance to sue (Sec 137).

flow.title: Modes of Surety Discharge
steps: Guarantee contract established
Creditor alters terms or releases debtor without surety consent
Creditor acts negligently impairing surety's eventual remedy
Surety gets completely discharged from liability
Creditor cannot recover unpaid debt from Surety

topics.example: Bank alters employee's salary and terms without surety's consent. Surety is discharged from liability for subsequent employee defaults.
remember: Variance without consent discharges surety for subsequent transactions (Sec 133)
Mere forbearance to sue debtor does NOT discharge surety (Sec 137)
Giving time via agreement with a 3rd party does NOT discharge surety (Sec 136)
mistakes: Believing mere delay or forbearance by creditor to sue debtor discharges the surety
Thinking variance in contract terms discharges surety for past acts before the variance

quiz.q: Under Section 133, any variance made in the terms of the contract without the surety's consent:
o: Discharges the surety for all transactions prior to the variance
Discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance
Has no legal impact on the surety's liability
Makes the contract of guarantee void from the beginning
quiz.why: Section 133 states variance without consent discharges the surety for all transactions taking place subsequent to such variance.

quiz.q: Does a creditor's mere forbearance (delay) to sue the principal debtor discharge the surety?
o: Yes, immediately after 30 days
Yes, under Section 134
No, under Section 137, mere forbearance does not discharge surety
Yes, if the debtor becomes insolvent during that time
quiz.why: Section 137 provides that mere forbearance to sue or enforce remedies does not discharge the surety unless agreed.

topics.title: Rights of a Surety
explain: Rights against Principal Debtor: Right of Subrogation (Sec 140 - steps into creditor's shoes after paying debt) and Implied Promise to Indemnify (Sec 145 - recover rightful payments made).
Rights against Creditor: Right to benefit of creditor's securities (Sec 141), Right to set-off, and Right to share reduction if debtor is insolvent.
Under Section 141, if creditor loses or parts with security without surety's consent, surety is discharged to the extent of security's value.
Rights against Co-sureties: Co-sureties are liable to contribute equally (Sec 146) unless contracted otherwise.
Under Section 147, co-sureties bound in different maximum sums must contribute equally as far as their limits permit.

flow.title: Right of Subrogation and Contribution
steps: Principal Debtor defaults on debt
Surety pays full guaranteed amount to Creditor
Surety steps into shoes of Creditor (Subrogation)
Surety inherits all securities held by Creditor
Surety claims equal contribution from Co-sureties

topics.example: A, B, C are sureties for D up to ₹1L, ₹2L, ₹4L. D defaults for ₹3L. Under Sec 147, A, B, and C pay ₹1L each.
remember: Subrogation = Surety steps into creditor's shoes after payment (Sec 140)
Creditor losing security discharges surety to the value of security lost (Sec 141)
Co-sureties pay equally up to their respective agreed limits (Sec 147)
mistakes: Thinking a surety can recover wrongful or improper payments from the principal debtor under Section 145
Assuming co-sureties with different limits contribute proportionally to limits instead of equally up to limits

quiz.q: The right of a surety to step into the shoes of the creditor upon paying the guaranteed debt is known as:
o: Right of indemnity
Right of subrogation
Right of contribution
Right of set-off
quiz.why: Section 140 defines the Right of Subrogation, where the surety gets invested with all rights of the creditor.

quiz.q: A, B, and C are sureties for D with maximum limits of ₹1,00,000, ₹2,00,000, and ₹4,00,000. D defaults for ₹4,00,000. How much must B and C pay?
o: A pays ₹1,00,000; B and C pay ₹1,50,000 each
A, B, and C pay ₹1,33,333 each
B pays ₹2,00,000 and C pays ₹2,00,000
A pays 0; B pays ₹2,00,000; C pays ₹2,00,000
quiz.why: Under Section 147, they contribute equally up to limits: A hits max limit of ₹1,00,000; remaining ₹3,00,000 is split equally between B and C (₹1,50,000 each).
